narrative: During the 2010s, Black and African women's hairstyles and hair culture continued to thrive, building on the momentum of previous decades. The natural hair movement, which originated in the 1960s and resurged in popularity in the 2000s, remained a powerful force, encouraging individuals to celebrate their kinky hair and reject Eurocentric beauty standards. Hairstyles like afros, cornrows, and box braids became increasingly popular, not only as a means of self-expression but also as a way to protect and preserve Afro-textured hair from damage caused by heat styling tools, chemical treatments, and environmental factors. Dreadlocks, Bantu knots, and locs were also worn with pride, reflecting the diversity and richness of African diasporic cultures. As part of this cultural renaissance, Black women's hairstyles became a symbol of resistance against racism and oppression, as well as a celebration of identity, community, and heritage. While documentation from this era is limited in the source material, it is clear that Black and African women's hair culture continued to evolve and flourish during the 2010s, reflecting their resilience, creativity, and commitment to self-love and empowerment.
